Rivers for sale

By: Anina Peens | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A thirsty city. A hidden trade. And water worth more than gold.

Unique Selling Point:
We follow the trucks no one is supposed to notice.
From hidden pumps to city streets, we trace the underground journey of Gqeberha’s water.


Summary:
In Gqeberha, a seemingly lucrative trade is brazenly thriving in the shadows. Tanker trucks move through suburbs and industrial areas, pumping and delivering thousands of litres of water every day to a city desperate for supply. But where this water comes from remains largely unseen. Our investigation reveals a brazen underground industry of opportunists drilling illegal boreholes, siphoning municipal water from fire hydrants and pumping from rivers and private properties before selling it across the metro. The trade has existed for years, but over the past year it has surged, fuelled by weak enforcement and few real consequences. Guided by an insider who knows the network but fears being identified, we follow the tankers to expose the hidden supply chain behind the city’s thirst.

Further information:
Over the past year, a brazen underground trade has taken hold. Opportunists are drilling unauthorised boreholes across the metro, extracting groundwater and selling it to any customer willing to pay. And they pay, because Port Elizabeth has gone dry. But even if the customers dont care whether their suppliers are legal suppliers or not, do they actually know where the water they buy are coming from?

Our investigation will reveal how illegal water tankers, pump water from rivers, and one of the biggest sources of for many illegal truckers, is the Baakenriver, that is so severely polluted that fish and birds are dying but this water, is sold as 'springwater'.

In other cases, illegal truckers get water from boreholes on private properties where licences only allow water to be used on site, not transported, let alone sold. Tankers have also been seen filling up directly from municipal fire hydrants. In areas where gang violence has taken a hold of communities, operators use the lack of law enforcement and the stigma of danger and gangland, to drain municipal water hydrants, knowing the chances are low that they might be caught.

Despite occasional enforcement, the business keeps growing. Operators may be fined but the penalties are often treated as part of the cost of doing business. With police stretched thin and demand rising, more players are entering the market.
Boreholes are drilled across the metro without authorisation, tapping into underground aquifers that experts warn are already under pressure. In some neighbourhoods, residents with boreholes have even begun piping water to surrounding homes and charging for supply.

At the centre of the story is an insider who knows the network of pumping sites across the city but fears being identified. He works for the municiaplaity, his job? Issuing licences for legal water providers. He knows exactly who is selling, who has licences and who not. He has been fighting a losing battle trying to get illegal operators off the road.

Our investigation will follow the trucks from source to delivery. We track where they pump water, watch where they drive and confront operators about their licences and permits. By physically following the tankers, we reveal the hidden supply chain that keeps thousands of litres flowing across the city every day.

It begins quietly: a hose stretched across a dry street, a resident waiting beside an empty tank, the low rumble of a water truck arriving. In a city where taps can run dry for weeks at a time, the tankers are often welcomed like saviours.

But as the investigation deepens, a darker picture begins to emerge. Tankers pull into abandoned industrial sites. Pumps roar beside polluted rivers. Hydrants are opened in quiet suburban streets long after midnight. Boreholes appear where there were none before. Groundwater is being drained.

And the question at the heart of the investigation becomes unavoidable:

In a city running dry, who is really controlling the water?

We will need 3 flights from Johannesburg to Port Elizabeth and return.

Press Release:


Rivers for Sale
A thirsty city. An underground trade. Water worth more than gold. In Gqeberha, when municipal supplies run low, illegal tankers move in, draining hundreds of thousands of litres from a system already strained by drought. As desperate residents pay for delivery, one question remains: where does the water come from? Carte Blanche exposes a brazen black market of illegal boreholes and siphoned municipal water. Guided by an insider, we trace the illicit journey of Gqeberha’s water to ask: in a city battling for every drop, who is really in control?
Producer: Anina Peens | Presenter: Govan Whittles

Script:


RIVERS FOR SALE FINAL
(Peter Hart) The business is lucrative when you’re doing those high volumes and it is extremely dangerous. There has been a guy and his wife that were murdered who were delivering water.
(Govan Whittles) Nelson Mandela Bay, a city at the epicentre of a growing battle over a contested resource, water.
(Govan Whittles) Is it a water black-market?
(Joseph Tsatsire) Yes, it is, it is.
(Govan Whittles) How big is it?
(Joseph Tsatsire) It is quite big. Most of the people that are selling water currently, they actually stealing it.
(Govan Whittles) In a country where water supply is often erratic, stealing it may seem an insignificant crime. Here, though, it’s taken on organised crime proportions.
(Shannon Barkes) I’ve got a funny feeling they know we’ve been watching them.
(Man with glasses) Get that camera out of my face.
(Govan Whittles) Is this your property sir?
(Man with glasses) dude, Get the fucking (BLEEP) camera out of my face.
(Govan Whittles) When the taps run dry, people are desperate for water and if someone is offering it to you at a discounted price in bulk, chances are, you’re gonna buy it. But do you know where it came from and what the real cost of that water may be?
(Shannon Barkes) The guy on that side where the double story house is, you will see there is a sump and the trucks they reverse in and they pump the water into the trucks.
(Govan Whittles) An official from the Nelson Mandela Bay Municipality takes us through Gqeberha.
(Shannon Barkes) You turn right at the street in front of you.
(Govan Whittles) Failing infrastructure and drought have left residents without reliable water and in that gap, illegal tankers have taken hold.
(Shannon Barkes) You can drive around anywhere, and you will see illegal truck, you will see them, everywhere.
(Govan Whittles) This is Malabar, near the city centre. It’s from here that much of the illegal water trade seems to be run. Boreholes are being drilled across the area, illegally tapping high volumes of water.
(Shannon Barkes) So, you can see there are one, two, three, four, five flow bins and each one of those is a thousand liters. So, its 5000 liters.
(Govan Whittles) Ground water is a protected national resource and selling it without a licence is illegal. Charging for transport is allowed, but again, only with a municipal licence. Here, issuing those licences is the responsibility of the officials showing us the hotspots. He’s hiding his face so illegal operators don’t see him coming.
(Govan Whittles) Here comes a, here comes a truck
(Shannon Barkes) Okay, he is legal guy, you can see the side of the truck he’s got the sticker on. If there is no sticker on the truck, you know it is illegal.
(Govan Whittles) You think people will be surprised to hear you cant sell borehole water?
(Shannon Barkes) I think a lot of people are unaware of it. It’s a thing that people don’t really understand.
(Govan Whittles) How much money can they make of this?
(Shannon Barkes) Up to hundred thousand a month.
(Govan Whittles) Hundred thousand a month, selling water?
(Shannon Barkes) yes, Selling water.
(Govan Whittles) He says they operate for seven days a week, with some owning as many as five trucks capable of carrying 5,000 litres each. We’re told each delivery fetches around R1300 on the black market. At that rate, a five-truck operation doing ten trips a day can make over R2 million a month, almost pure profit.
(Shannon Barkes) that is an illegal truck there, it has got no stickers on, lets follow it. They are doing a circle here, that means they know we are watching them. They won’t deliver now. They won’t deliver.
(Govan Whittles) The driver sees our cameras, so we turn down a side street to wait it out.
(Shannon Barkes) Hang on, what the hell is going on here?
(Govan Whittles) Vehicles fitted with flow bins are parked everywhere.
(Govan Whittles) There’s another truck, and this is a sector policing…
(Govan Whittles) It’s an odd sight: a policing vehicle, deployed to increase visible policing, with a large flow bin mounted on its back.
(Govan Whittles) Water is big business in Malabar.
(Shannon Barkes) It’s big business throughout the city.
(Govan Whittles) And the water isn’t only taken from boreholes. These photos show water tankers being filled from rivers known for pollution. With little consequence, operators have become increasingly brazen.
(Caller) Hallo
(Govan Whittles) Howzit, I got your number on Facebook marketplace for the water.
(Caller) Yes, yes.
(Govan Whittles) Ja, I’m uhm I need some water to fill up my pool. And I need potable water, drinking water, can you do that?
(Caller) Yes, yes, How many liters of water do you need?
(Govan Whittles) This operator is available to deliver anywhere, any time.
(Caller) I can bring like, 4000 at a time.
(Govan Whittles) Would you be able to send me just your, your registration number to transport the water, on, on WhatsApp?
(Caller) Registration number of the vehicle?
(Govan Whittles) No, to transport the water. You’re licensed to sell the water, right? to transport it?
(Caller) Yes.
(Govan Whittles) You do have the stickers on the side of your water truck, don’t you?
(Caller) Ja, not on the new truck now, the other truck is at the Bodyshop.
(Govan Whittles) Nelson Mandela Bay Municipal Head of Infrastructure says there’s no way to stop it, but that the perpetrators should be jailed.
(Joseph Tsatsire) We are looking into reviewing our by-law to criminalize that element. Because obviously the fines that is currently in our by-law regime it is less punitive. People, even if you catch them doing that, they pay a very little amount.
(Govan Whittles) This is the stream ja?
(Peter Hart) Yes, when it rains and stuff
(Govan Whittles) Peter Hart is one of only six licensed suppliers.
(Peter Hart) I’ve got a spring on my property and that is why I eventually got a license, because it’s surface water. One of the things that had to be done was a hydro geological study. That was thousands and thousands of Rands.
(Govan Whittles) He says every supply failure by the municipality is an opportunity for illegal operators.
(Peter Hart) A little while ago, my phone crashed because of all the calls coming through. This town had no water, and it was chaos.
(Govan Whittles) Is this the kind of business that could put your life in danger?
(Peter Hart) I would say more towards the bigger guys that are delivering. There was a guy delivering with a huge water tanker, he was murdered by the very guy that was helping them deliver water. And I know a large sum of money was taken in that murder.
(Govan Whittles) Peter is too nervous to tell us where the illegal suppliers operate from, but knowing Malibar is a hotspot, we head back there. A few minutes in, we’re on the trail of another illegal carrier.

(Govan Whittles) Heyta. Sharp.
(Govan Whittles) Are you licensed to sell water?
(Driver) Yes, I’m gonna show you everything.
(Govan Whittles) He is calling his boss.
(Driver) Please don’t videorise me sir, please.
(Govan Whittles) Minutes later, a second truck arrives, another five thousand litres.
(Shannon Barkes) Hi, I am from the municipality. Have you got a permit to transport water? Can I se it?
(Man with grey hair) Why are you guys bombarding me here?
(Govan Whittles) No, we, Im from Carte Blanche my name is Govan. Nice to meet you ja, we’re doing a story of water and the transportation of water in PE.
(Man with grey hair) Okay, I was just telling this gentleman now, we are not selling the water so we are pumping the water from our borehole.
(Govan Whittles) So these are your two trucks?
(Man with grey hair) yes sir.
(Govan Whittles) Really?
(Man with grey hair) yes sir.
(Govan Whittles) Cause the driver of that truck was just calling the owner now and it was a different person.
(Man with grey hair) no I am not the owner.
(Govan Whittles) Another man arrives, clearly the one in charge. He says he’s just security, but it doesn’t hold.
(Man with glasses) Get the camera out of my face.
(Govan Whittles) No, they are filming, is this, is this your property sir?
(Man with glasses) I’m the security on this property.
(Govan Whittles) Do you know if this is legal water, do you know where it came from?
(Man with glasses) It came from boreholes.
(Govan Whittles) Which boreholes?
(Man with glasses) All over Malibar.
(Govan Whittles) Okay, you know you’re not allowed to transport borehole water off the property?
(Man with glasses) I’ve inspected by the municipality four times and they have given us the go-ahead to transport water off site.
(Shannon Barkes) Who gave you the authority.
(Man with glasses) The people from the municipality
(Shannon Barkes) I am the only one who does that.
(Govan Whittles) It turns out, though, that he doesn’t believe in regulation at all!
(Man with glasses) It is the creators water because it is coming from his earth.
(Govan Whittles) For sure
(Man with glasses) And it does not belong to the municipality.
(Govan Whittles) And who regulates its movement?
(Man with glasses) Why do they need to regulate something that doesn’t belong to them?
(Man with glasses) Am I taking from the dams? Am I taking from the municipality? I am taking from a natural resource
(Govan Whittles) The water table, I understand.
(Man with glasses) Does it affect the municipality in any way, shape or form?
(Shannon Barkes) Yes, it does.
(Man with glasses) How?
(Shannon Barkes) Because we spend millions of Rands drilling boreholes to secure water for all the people in the metro during the drought, now you hammering the water table that drops the water table and then we don’t get water out of our boreholes.
(Govan Whittles) The municipality says water theft benefits only a few, while others in the city are left to suffer as shared reserves are drained.
(Joseph Tsatsire) You can take for example, minerals in the country, they also come from the creator, from the state. But for your to be able to extract them, you require a license.
(Govan Whittles) What’s happening in Gqeberha isn’t isolated. As our water crisis deepens, the risk is no longer just a shortage, but who controls what’s left.

(Caller) Registration number of the vehicle? (Govan Whittles) No, to transport the water. You’re licensed to sell the water, right? to transport it? (Caller) Yes. (Govan Whittles) You do have the stickers on the side of your water truck, don’t you? (Caller) Ja, not on the new truck now, the other truck is at the Bodyshop. (Govan Whittles) Nelson Mandela Bay Municipal Head of Infrastructure says there’s no way to stop it, but that the perpetrators should be jailed. (Joseph Tsatsire) We are looking into reviewing our by-law to criminalize that element. Because obviously the fines that is currently in our by-law regime it is less punitive. People, even if you catch them doing that, they pay a very little amount. (Govan Whittles) This is the stream ja? (Peter Hart) Yes, when it rains and stuff (Govan Whittles) Peter Hart is one of only six licensed suppliers. (Peter Hart) I’ve got a spring on my property and that is why I eventually got a license, because it’s surface water. One of the things that had to be done was a hydro geological study. That was thousands and thousands of Rands. (Govan Whittles) He says every supply failure by the municipality is an opportunity for illegal operators. (Peter Hart) A little while ago, my phone crashed because of all the calls coming through. This town had no water, and it was chaos. (Govan Whittles) Is this the kind of business that could put your life in danger? (Peter Hart) I would say more towards the bigger guys that are delivering. There was a guy delivering with a huge water tanker, he was murdered by the very guy that was helping them deliver water. And I know a large sum of money was taken in that murder. (Govan Whittles) Peter is too nervous to tell us where the illegal suppliers operate from, but knowing Malibar is a hotspot, we head back there. A few minutes in, we’re on the trail of another illegal carrier. (Govan Whittles) Heyta. Sharp. (Govan Whittles) Are you licensed to sell water? (Driver) Yes, I’m gonna show you everything. (Govan Whittles) He is calling his boss. (Driver) Please don’t videorise me sir, please. (Govan Whittles) Minutes later, a second truck arrives, another five thousand litres. (Shannon Barkes) Hi, I am from the municipality. Have you got a permit to transport water? Can I se it? (Man with grey hair) Why are you guys bombarding me here? (Govan Whittles) No, we, Im from Carte Blanche my name is Govan. Nice to meet you ja, we’re doing a story of water and the transportation of water in PE. (Man with grey hair) Okay, I was just telling this gentleman now, we are not selling the water so we are pumping the water from our borehole. (Govan Whittles) So these are your two trucks? (Man with grey hair) yes sir. (Govan Whittles) Really? (Man with grey hair) yes sir. (Govan Whittles) Cause the driver of that truck was just calling the owner now and it was a different person. (Man with grey hair) no I am not the owner. (Govan Whittles) Another man arrives, clearly the one in charge. He says he’s just security, but it doesn’t hold. (Man with glasses) Get the camera out of my face. (Govan Whittles) No, they are filming, is this, is this your property sir? (Man with glasses) I’m the security on this property. (Govan Whittles) Do you know if this is legal water, do you know where it came from? (Man with glasses) It came from boreholes. (Govan Whittles) Which boreholes? (Man with glasses) All over Malibar. (Govan Whittles) Okay, you know you’re not allowed to transport borehole water off the property? (Man with glasses) I’ve inspected by the municipality four times and they have given us the go-ahead to transport water off site. (Shannon Barkes) Who gave you the authority. (Man with glasses) The people from the municipality (Shannon Barkes) I am the only one who does that. (Govan Whittles) It turns out, though, that he doesn’t believe in regulation at all! (Man with glasses) It is the creators water because it is coming from his earth. (Govan Whittles) For sure (Man with glasses) And it does not belong to the municipality. (Govan Whittles) And who regulates its movement? (Man with glasses) Why do they need to regulate something that doesn’t belong to them? (Man with glasses) Am I taking from the dams? Am I taking from the municipality? I am taking from a natural resource (Govan Whittles) The water table, I understand. (Man with glasses) Does it affect the municipality in any way, shape or form? (Shannon Barkes) Yes, it does. (Man with glasses) How? (Shannon Barkes) Because we spend millions of Rands drilling boreholes to secure water for all the people in the metro during the drought, now you hammering the water table that drops the water table and then we don’t get water out of our boreholes. (Govan Whittles) The municipality says water theft benefits only a few, while others in the city are left to suffer as shared reserves are drained. (Joseph Tsatsire) You can take for example, minerals in the country, they also come from the creator, from the state. But for your to be able to extract them, you require a license. (Govan Whittles) What’s happening in Gqeberha isn’t isolated. As our water crisis deepens, the risk is no longer just a shortage, but who controls what’s left.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A thirsty city. A hidden trade. And water worth more than gold.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We follow the trucks no one is supposed to notice. From hidden pumps to city streets, we trace the underground journey of Gqeberha’s water.
metadata.Summary: In Gqeberha, a seemingly lucrative trade is brazenly thriving in the shadows. Tanker trucks move through suburbs and industrial areas, pumping and delivering thousands of litres of water every day to a city desperate for supply. But where this water comes from remains largely unseen. Our investigation reveals a brazen underground industry of opportunists drilling illegal boreholes, siphoning municipal water from fire hydrants and pumping from rivers and private properties before selling it across the metro. The trade has existed for years, but over the past year it has surged, fuelled by weak enforcement and few real consequences. Guided by an insider who knows the network but fears being identified, we follow the tankers to expose the hidden supply chain behind the city’s thirst.
metadata.Further information: Over the past year, a brazen underground trade has taken hold. Opportunists are drilling unauthorised boreholes across the metro, extracting groundwater and selling it to any customer willing to pay. And they pay, because Port Elizabeth has gone dry. But even if the customers dont care whether their suppliers are legal suppliers or not, do they actually know where the water they buy are coming from? Our investigation will reveal how illegal water tankers, pump water from rivers, and one of the biggest sources of for many illegal truckers, is the Baakenriver, that is so severely polluted that fish and birds are dying but this water, is sold as 'springwater'. In other cases, illegal truckers get water from boreholes on private properties where licences only allow water to be used on site, not transported, let alone sold. Tankers have also been seen filling up directly from municipal fire hydrants. In areas where gang violence has taken a hold of communities, operators use the lack of law enforcement and the stigma of danger and gangland, to drain municipal water hydrants, knowing the chances are low that they might be caught. Despite occasional enforcement, the business keeps growing. Operators may be fined but the penalties are often treated as part of the cost of doing business. With police stretched thin and demand rising, more players are entering the market. Boreholes are drilled across the metro without authorisation, tapping into underground aquifers that experts warn are already under pressure. In some neighbourhoods, residents with boreholes have even begun piping water to surrounding homes and charging for supply. At the centre of the story is an insider who knows the network of pumping sites across the city but fears being identified. He works for the municiaplaity, his job? Issuing licences for legal water providers. He knows exactly who is selling, who has licences and who not. He has been fighting a losing battle trying to get illegal operators off the road. Our investigation will follow the trucks from source to delivery. We track where they pump water, watch where they drive and confront operators about their licences and permits. By physically following the tankers, we reveal the hidden supply chain that keeps thousands of litres flowing across the city every day. It begins quietly: a hose stretched across a dry street, a resident waiting beside an empty tank, the low rumble of a water truck arriving. In a city where taps can run dry for weeks at a time, the tankers are often welcomed like saviours. But as the investigation deepens, a darker picture begins to emerge. Tankers pull into abandoned industrial sites. Pumps roar beside polluted rivers. Hydrants are opened in quiet suburban streets long after midnight. Boreholes appear where there were none before. Groundwater is being drained. And the question at the heart of the investigation becomes unavoidable: In a city running dry, who is really controlling the water?
